title: ropeway:handbook-title-52
text: A ropeway does not run on nothing. It runs on a tension weight: a mass wound up its guide by mechanical power, whose stored energy is what actually hauls the cabin. Mechanical power winds the weight; the weight moves the cabin. The wind never touches the ride directly, and that is the point. Building the drive 1. Run an axle to any pylon footing on the line. It takes power on either side of the crossarm - the same axis the crossarm runs along, never down the line the cabin travels - and its block info panel tells you the speed it is turning at. 2. Build one tension weight within eight blocks of any tower on the same line. One per line, and it serves the whole line no matter which tower it stands beside. A windmill, a water wheel, anything on a vanilla mechanical network will do - a five-sail wooden windmill in good wind winds about a block and a half of travel every second, so a level hundred-block trip is a little over a minute of winding. Nothing here is metal-gated: a wooden windmill rotor, wooden axles and angled gears cost no metal at all. Any tower can take power, and they add up There is no drive station. Put the drive where the terrain suits it - wind on a ridge, water in the valley - and if one mill is not enough, power a second tower somewhere else along the route. Every powered tower winds the same weight, so their contributions pool. Intermediate drive stations were real on long ropeways for exactly this reason: driving the haul loop anywhere along its length drives all of it. Trips are paid for before they start When the cabin leaves a station it is quoted a cost in blocks of travel and the tension weight pays it in full, up front: the line's length, dearer for a net climb and cheaper for a net descent, so a downhill ore line is genuinely cheap to run. Because the trip is already paid for, a journey that starts always finishes. The wind can drop, the mill can stall, the whole drive tower can go out of sight into unloaded chunks, and the cabin you are sitting in carries on at its usual pace. What a dead calm costs you is the next departure, and the tower panel tells you the shortfall as a number rather than leaving you guessing. Dead calm Vanilla weather goes still for hours at a time and no windmill of any size makes torque then. That is what the weight is for: wind it while the wind blows and ride while it does not. If you want to smooth out the lulls further, a flywheel on the axle line stores rotational energy and pays it back when torque drops - it is an ordinary node on the mechanical network, so the ropeway neither knows nor cares that it is there. Useful, never required. Back to Aerial Ropeways.
